## Where we are

In part 1 you put a repository online and wrote a `README.md`. That README was
markdown, which is the first of the three formats we are going to look at.

In this part we take that idea and add code to it, so that a document can
compute its own contents.

## The problem

A familiar sequence: you run an analysis, copy the numbers into a manuscript,
and make a plot that you export and insert. Then a reviewer asks you to exclude
a few participants.

Now every number and every figure has to be found and replaced by hand, and the
only thing standing between you and a wrong number in print is your own
carefulness at five in the afternoon.

## The idea

Keep the text and the code in the same file, and let the document produce its
own numbers and figures when you render it.

Re-running the analysis and updating the manuscript become the same action. A
stale number is not something you have to be careful about; it becomes something
that cannot happen.

## Three formats

| | what it is | when |
|---|---|---|
| **`.md`** | plain text with simple formatting | since 2004 |
| **`.Rmd`** | markdown + R code chunks | 2012, R only |
| **`.qmd`** | the same idea, rebuilt and generalised | 2022, Quarto |

We will spend most of the time on Quarto, but the progression matters: each one
adds a single thing to the one before it.

## Markdown

Plain text that carries structure. You already wrote some.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```md
## A heading

Some *emphasis* and some
**strong emphasis**.

- a list
- of things

[a link](https://quarto.org)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
It is readable as text, so a diff in git is meaningful — you can see which
sentence changed.

That is not true of `.docx`, which is why this matters for us.
:::
:::

## R Markdown adds code chunks

````{.markdown}
The dataset has 87 characters.

```{{r}}
starwars |> count(species, sort = TRUE)
```
````

The chunk runs when you render, and its output lands in the document. Knit the
file and you get an HTML, PDF or Word file with the results already in place.

## And inline code

This is the part worth slowing down for.

```{.markdown}
The dataset has `r nrow(starwars)` characters,
of whom `r sum(starwars$species == "Droid", na.rm = TRUE)` are droids.
```

renders as

> The dataset has 87 characters, of whom 6 are droids.

Numbers in your sentences are computed, not typed. Change the data, re-render,
and the prose is correct again.

## Quarto

Quarto is the same idea rebuilt. R Markdown is an R package; Quarto is a
standalone program that also handles Python, Julia and Observable, and does not
need R installed to run.

For our purposes the day-to-day differences are small, and an `.Rmd` will
usually render as a `.qmd` unchanged. Three things are worth knowing.

## 1. YAML at the top

```yaml
---
title: "Do bigger characters weigh more?"
author: "Your name"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    embed-resources: true
---
```

Everything about the output is configured here rather than in the code. The same
document can be rendered to several formats by changing these few lines.

## 2. Chunk options moved inside

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**R Markdown**

````{.markdown}
```{{r plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4}}
```
````
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Quarto**

````{.markdown}
```{{r}}
#| label: plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
```
````
:::
:::

Options now live in the chunk body, one per line, prefixed with `#|`. It is more
typing, but it does not run off the edge of the screen and it is easier to
comment out a single option.

## 3. The options you will actually use

| option | effect |
|---|---|
| `label` | names the chunk; use it, it makes errors findable |
| `echo: false` | run the code, hide it |
| `eval: false` | show the code, do not run it |
| `warning: false`, `message: false` | keep library chatter out of the report |
| `fig-cap` | caption, and makes the figure cross-referenceable |

Set them for the whole document in the YAML, or per chunk when you need an
exception.

## Your turn

`exercises/02_literate/02a_build_a_report.qmd`

You will build a short report on the `starwars` data that ships with dplyr,
asking whether taller characters weigh more.

Eight tasks. Some ask for code, some ask you to write prose. The alternation is
deliberate — a report is an argument with evidence in it, not a script with
comments.

## Publishing

When you are happy with it, render into `docs/`, commit, and push.

You switched GitHub Pages on in part 1, so the placeholder page you saw then
will be replaced by your report. It can take a minute to update.

That URL is how your partner will read your work in part 3.

## What we have not covered

Quarto does considerably more than this: cross-references, citations from a
`.bib` file, parameterised reports, multi-page websites, books, and the slides
you are looking at right now.

The documentation at <https://quarto.org> is genuinely good, and the place to
start is the guide rather than the reference.
